pages.title: What Are Design Patterns
pages.summary: A design pattern is a named, proven solution to a design problem that keeps coming back, described so you can adapt it rather than copy it. The classic catalogue is the Gang of Four's 23 patterns, grouped into creational, structural and behavioural. Learn them to recognise problems faster and to talk about designs in a few words.

pages.title: Why Patterns Matter (and When They Don't)
pages.summary: Patterns matter because they give teams a shared vocabulary and proven ways to keep code easy to change. They stop mattering, and start hurting, when you add them for changes that never come. Modern Java has made several patterns much smaller, so the goal is the pattern's intent, not its original class diagram.

pages.title: Setting Up Java to Run the Examples
pages.summary: Install a JDK 21, check it with `java -version`, and you can run every example in this playbook with `java File.java`. Use Maven when an example has several files or tests, and JShell when you want to try one line. Any major IDE works.

pages.title: Reading UML for Patterns
pages.summary: Every pattern page shows its structure as a UML class diagram and its behaviour as a sequence diagram. You need about a dozen symbols to read them: boxes for classes and interfaces, six kinds of lines for relationships, and arrows for calls over time. This page maps each symbol to the Java code that produces it.

pages.title: OOP Refresher for Patterns
pages.summary: Every design pattern is a particular arrangement of four OOP ideas: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism. If you can hide state behind methods, depend on interfaces, and choose composition over inheritance by default, most patterns stop looking like magic and start looking like common sense.

pages.title: SOLID Principles
pages.summary: SOLID is five principles for classes that are easy to change: one reason to change per class, extend without editing, subtypes that keep their parent's promises, small interfaces, and dependencies on abstractions. They are the "why" behind most design patterns: when you can name which principle a design breaks, you usually know which pattern fixes it.

pages.title: DRY, KISS, YAGNI and Friends
pages.summary: SOLID tells you how to make code flexible; DRY, KISS and YAGNI stop you overdoing it. Keep each piece of *knowledge* in one place (DRY), choose the simplest design that works (KISS), and don't build what nobody needs yet (YAGNI). Law of Demeter, Tell Don't Ask, cohesion/coupling and GRASP help you decide which class a piece of behaviour belongs to.

pages.title: Singleton
pages.summary: Singleton guarantees a class has exactly one instance and gives global access to it. In Java the safest forms are an `enum` or the lazy holder idiom. Use it sparingly: global state hurts testing and hides dependencies, so in most applications you want *one instance created in the composition root and injected*, not the Singleton pattern itself.

pages.title: Factory Method
pages.summary: Factory Method moves the decision "which class do I create?" out of the code that uses the object. In the classic form a base class calls an abstract `create...()` method that subclasses override. In everyday Java you'll more often see its relatives: static factory methods (`List.of`, `Money.ofCents`), parameterised factories (`switch` on a kind) and `Supplier<T>`. Use it when the concrete type varies; skip it when `new` is clear and stable.

pages.title: Builder
pages.summary: Builder constructs a complex object step by step, so callers name each value they set, optional fields get defaults, and validation runs once in `build()` before an immutable object exists. Use it when a constructor would take many parameters, several of them optional. In modern Java, pair it with records; for two or three fields, a constructor or static factory is better.

pages.title: Strategy
pages.summary: Strategy puts each variant of an algorithm (how to price, sort, assign, round) behind one interface, so the code that uses it can swap algorithms without `if/else` chains. In Java 8+ a strategy is often just a lambda (`Comparator` is the most famous example). It's the pattern you'll use most; the hard parts are choosing the strategy at runtime and rolling new ones out safely.

pages.title: Observer
pages.summary: Observer lets one object (the subject) notify any number of others (observers) when something happens, without knowing who they are. It's how "order placed" reaches inventory, email and loyalty without checkout calling each one. The pattern is easy; the production questions are hard: sync or async, what happens when an observer fails, and who unsubscribes.

pages.title: Template Method
pages.summary: Template Method fixes the steps of an algorithm in one `final` method of a base class and lets subclasses fill in the steps that vary. It's how frameworks keep the important parts (transactions, retries, validation) in one place while you supply the business bits. In modern Java, passing the varying steps as lambdas often does the same job without inheritance.

pages.title: Adapter
pages.summary: Adapter makes an existing class (a vendor SDK, a legacy library) usable through the interface your code expects, by wrapping it and translating calls, data and errors. It's the everyday tool for integrating third parties without letting their types, units and error codes leak into your domain. Prefer object adapters (composition); test every adapter against one shared contract.

pages.title: Decorator
pages.summary: Decorator adds behaviour to an object by wrapping it in another object with the same interface. Each wrapper adds one concern (caching, retries, logging, discounts), and wrappers stack in any order at runtime, which avoids a subclass for every combination. `java.io` streams are the classic example; resilience stacks (retry, circuit breaker, metrics) are the everyday production one.

pages.title: Facade
pages.summary: Facade gives a complicated set of classes one simple entry point for a common task, like "place order" or "get delivery quote". The client calls one method; the facade coordinates the subsystems in the right order. Keep facades focused on one use-case area, keep business rules in services or the domain, and use facades as the public face of modules.

pages.title: Abstract Factory
pages.summary: Abstract Factory is an interface for creating a *family* of related objects (tax rules, address format and delivery promise for a country; charge, webhook and refund clients for an environment) without naming their classes. Pick one concrete factory, usually at startup, and every object it creates is guaranteed to match. Its weakness: adding a new kind of product changes every factory.
